title: AP Statistics Independent Foundation Pilot
description: An independently authored 240-question AP Statistics foundation pilot spanning the five revised Fall 2026 units. It tests the blueprint crosswalk, statistical-practice metadata, native learning routes, and unscored response planning before any official or release-ready expansion.
disclaimer: Independent, unofficial AP Statistics preparation material for internal foundation-pilot development only. Not affiliated with, endorsed by, or authored by College Board. This pilot does not provide official scores, score predictions, college-credit predictions, or automated FRQ scores.
previewBadge: Internal foundation pilot - 240 original draft items
contentReview: Two hundred forty original source-aligned draft multiple-choice items distributed evenly across the five revised Fall 2026 units and all fifty-five public framework topics, with transfer depth beyond the two-item topic floor. Native study routes cover five chapters, fifteen section-linked practice routes, four guided cumulative routes, and five original unit quick references; nine constructed-response planning workshops are explicitly unscored. Independent AP Statistics subject-expert review, rights review, accessibility review, production validation, field testing, and psychometric calibration remain pending.

items.prompt: Which question is a valid statistical investigative question?
choices: What share of students at this school walk or bike?
Did Maya walk to school on Tuesday morning last week?
What is the name of the school mascot chosen for this year?
Is walking always better than driving for every student?
items.rationale: A statistical investigative question anticipates variability and identifies a population or sample from which data can be collected.
choiceRationales: Best answer. A statistical investigative question anticipates variability and identifies a population or sample from which data can be collected.
This asks about one person on one day, so there is no variability to investigate and no population to describe.
Naming the school mascot asks for a single fixed fact with one deterministic answer, whereas a valid statistical investigative question anticipates variability across a group of individuals.
This is an opinion question about every student, not a measurable characteristic that varies and can be estimated from data.

items.learningSectionLabel: One-Variable Data and Collecting Data: study route 1

items.prompt: A study records the number of text messages sent by each participant. Which variable is quantitative?
choices: The participant’s favorite messaging app
The participant’s total SMS count
Whether the participant has a phone
The participant’s grade level
items.rationale: A quantitative variable records a measured or counted numerical amount with meaningful units.
choiceRationales: A favorite app is a category label, so the variable is categorical, not a counted or measured amount.
Best answer. A quantitative variable records a measured or counted numerical amount with meaningful units.
Recording whether someone owns a phone yields a binary yes-or-no label rather than a numerical measurement with units, so it is a categorical variable instead of a quantitative one.
Grade level names a group a student belongs to; even when written as a number it functions as a category here.

items.prompt: In a survey of 240 students, 84 choose the later lunch period. What is the relative frequency for that category?
items.rationale: Relative frequency is the category count divided by the total count: 84/240 = 0.35.
choiceRationales: 0.28 would be 84 out of 300; the survey had 240 students, so the relative frequency is 84/240 = 0.35.
0.65 is the complement 1 − 0.35, which gives the proportion of surveyed students who did not pick the later lunch period rather than the 84 out of 240 who actually chose it.
Best answer. Relative frequency is the category count divided by the total count: 84/240 = 0.35.
2.86 comes from dividing the total by the category count (240/84); relative frequency divides the other way and must be at most 1.

items.prompt: Which display is most appropriate for showing the counts of transportation methods used by students?
choices: A histogram
A scatterplot
A boxplot
A bar chart
items.rationale: Transportation method is categorical, so a bar chart displays the count or relative frequency of each category.
choiceRationales: Histograms group a quantitative variable into contiguous numerical intervals on a scaled axis, whereas student transportation methods are distinct categories that belong on a bar chart.
A scatterplot shows the relationship between two quantitative variables, and here there is one categorical variable.
Boxplots summarize a quantitative distribution using ordered quartiles, median, and extremes, which cannot be computed for unordered categorical labels like transportation modes.
Best answer. Transportation method is categorical, so a bar chart displays the count or relative frequency of each category.

items.learningObjectiveLabel: Graphical Representations for One Categorical Variable
items.learningSectionLabel: One-Variable Data and Collecting Data: study route 1

items.prompt: A histogram of commute times peaks between 10 and 25 minutes with a long upper tail of high values. How should the distribution be described?
choices: Unimodal and skewed right
Uniform and symmetric
Bimodal and skewed left
Unimodal and exactly normal
items.rationale: The concentration near smaller values with a longer tail toward larger values indicates right skewness; the single main peak is unimodal.
choiceRationales: Best answer. The concentration near smaller values with a longer tail toward larger values indicates right skewness; the single main peak is unimodal.
A uniform shape has no peak and equal heights; this histogram has a clear concentration between 10 and 25 minutes and a long tail.
The commute-time histogram shows a single prominent peak rather than two separate modes, and its stretched tail of unusually long times extends to the right, indicating right skewness.
A normal shape is symmetric; a long right tail rules out normality even though the distribution has one peak.

items.prompt: Which statistic is generally most resistant to an unusually large outlier in a quantitative distribution?
choices: The mean
The median
The standard deviation
The range
items.rationale: The median and IQR are resistant summaries; a very large value can pull the mean and increase the range and standard deviation.
choiceRationales: Because computing the arithmetic mean sums every observation in the data set, a single unusually large outlier pulls the average noticeably upward instead of leaving it steady.
Best answer. The median and IQR are resistant summaries; a very large value can pull the mean and increase the range and standard deviation.
Standard deviation squares each distance from the mean, so a single extreme value inflates it substantially.
The range equals the maximum value minus the minimum value, so adding one unusually large observation stretches the maximum directly and inflates the entire spread measure.

items.prompt: A distribution has mean 52 and standard deviation 6. What is the z-score for an observation of 64?
items.rationale: The z-score is (64 − 52)/6 = 2, so the observation is two standard deviations above the mean.
choiceRationales: A negative z-score would mean the observation is below the mean; 64 is above 52, so the sign is positive.
0.5 is the standard deviation divided by the distance (6/12); the z-score divides the distance by the standard deviation, 12/6 = 2.
Best answer. The z-score is (64 − 52)/6 = 2, so the observation is two standard deviations above the mean.
12 is only the raw deviation above the mean (64 − 52); converting that difference to a standardized z-score requires dividing by the standard deviation of 6 to obtain 2.

items.prompt: A boxplot has minimum 4, first quartile 9, median 13, third quartile 18, and maximum 27. What is the interquartile range?
items.rationale: The interquartile range measures the spread of the middle 50% of a distribution using IQR = Q3 - Q1. Ignoring the minimum, median, and maximum, subtracting Q1 = 9 from Q3 = 18 gives 18 - 9 = 9.
choiceRationales: 5 equals Q1 minus the minimum (9 − 4), which gives the span of the lower whisker in the bottom quarter rather than the spread of the central 50% between Q1 and Q3.
14 subtracts the minimum from the third quartile (18 − 4), combining the lowest three quarters instead of isolating the interquartile range by subtracting Q1 from Q3.
23 equals the overall range from maximum to minimum (27 − 4), measuring total spread across every observation rather than the interquartile range spanning the middle half.

Best answer. The interquartile range measures the spread of the middle 50% of a distribution using IQR = Q3 - Q1. Ignoring the minimum, median, and maximum, subtracting Q1 = 9 from Q3 = 18 gives 18 - 9 = 9.

items.learningObjectiveLabel: Graphical Representations of Summary Statistics for One Quantitative Variable
items.learningSectionLabel: One-Variable Data and Collecting Data: study route 2

items.prompt: Two classes have the same median test score. Class A has a smaller IQR than Class B. What does that indicate?
choices: The middle half of Class A scores is less spread.
Class A must therefore have the larger mean score.
Class A has more of its scores below the median.
Class B must therefore have a higher maximum score.
items.rationale: The IQR measures the spread of the middle half of a distribution; it does not determine the mean or the extremes.
choiceRationales: Best answer. The IQR measures the spread of the middle half of a distribution; it does not determine the mean or the extremes.
The IQR measures spread of the middle half and says nothing about the mean; equal medians with different IQRs are consistent with any ordering of means.
By definition roughly half of the scores in any class fall below its median; a smaller interquartile range reflects tighter clustering in the middle 50%, not a higher share below the median.
A larger IQR means a wider middle half, but the maximum is an extreme value the IQR does not determine.

items.prompt: A researcher changes the wording of a survey question after seeing that the first wording produced an unexpected result. Why is that a problem?
choices: It ensures that the study will end up with a much larger random sample of people.
Editing items once data are known lets early outcomes steer the inquiry.
It turns an observational study into a fully randomized experiment instead.
It eliminates all of the response bias from every one of the survey responses given.
items.rationale: A valid investigative question should be determined before the analysis so the study is not retrofitted to a desired or surprising result.
choiceRationales: Altering a survey prompt after inspecting responses neither increases the number of participants nor makes their selection random; sample size and sampling design are set separately.
Best answer. A valid investigative question should be determined before the analysis so the study is not retrofitted to a desired or surprising result.
Conducting a randomized experiment requires actively imposing treatments through random assignment to subjects, whereas revising survey wording after seeing data remains observational.
Adjusting question phrasing to pursue a desired pattern introduces wording and confirmation bias into responses rather than removing systematic measurement error from the survey.

items.prompt: A school divides its students by grade level and selects a simple random sample from each grade. Which sampling method is used?
choices: A cluster random sample
A voluntary response sample
A stratified random sample
A systematic sample
items.rationale: Strata are groups formed before sampling, and a random sample is taken from every stratum.
choiceRationales: Cluster sampling selects whole groups and surveys everyone inside them; here every grade contributes a random sample, which is stratification.
Voluntary response lets people opt in on their own; this design uses random selection within each grade.
Best answer. Strata are groups formed before sampling, and a random sample is taken from every stratum.
A systematic sample takes every kth person from a list after a random start; no such rule is used here.

items.learningObjectiveLabel: Sampling Methods
items.learningSectionLabel: One-Variable Data and Collecting Data: study route 3

items.prompt: A city randomly selects three entire neighborhoods and surveys every household in those neighborhoods. Which sampling method is used?
choices: A stratified random sample
A convenience sample
A census of the city
A cluster random sample
items.rationale: Clusters are whole naturally occurring groups selected at random; all or many units within selected clusters are then observed.
choiceRationales: Stratified sampling takes a random sample from every group; here only three neighborhoods are chosen and then fully surveyed.
Although whole neighborhoods are surveyed together, those three neighborhoods were chosen through random selection rather than picked simply because they were nearby or easy to reach.
A true census attempts to gather data from every household across the entire city, whereas this design surveys only the households located inside three randomly chosen neighborhoods.
Best answer. Clusters are whole naturally occurring groups selected at random; all or many units within selected clusters are then observed.

items.learningSectionLabel: One-Variable Data and Collecting Data: study route 3

items.prompt: A poll about school start times is posted on a website, and anyone may choose to respond. Which bias is especially likely?
choices: Voluntary response bias
Undercoverage caused by a census
Placebo bias
Regression to the mean
items.rationale: People who choose to respond may have stronger opinions than the target population, producing voluntary response bias.
choiceRationales: Best answer. People who choose to respond may have stronger opinions than the target population, producing voluntary response bias.
A census includes everyone, so it does not cause undercoverage, and no census is involved in an open web poll.
Placebo effects arise in experiments when participants respond to an inactive treatment, whereas an open online poll imposes no treatment and suffers instead from self-selected respondents.
Regression to the mean concerns extreme measurements moving toward average on remeasurement, not who chooses to answer a poll.

items.learningObjectiveLabel: Sources of Bias in Data Collection
items.learningSectionLabel: One-Variable Data and Collecting Data: study route 3

items.prompt: A survey of residents is conducted only in English even though a large part of the population speaks other languages. What concern is most direct?
choices: Type I error
Undercoverage bias
Response variable bias
Random assignment
items.rationale: Some members of the target population have little or no chance to be included, which is undercoverage.
choiceRationales: A Type I error is a hypothesis-testing mistake of rejecting a true null hypothesis, whereas excluding non-English speakers from a survey creates a sampling-frame coverage flaw.
Best answer. Some members of the target population have little or no chance to be included, which is undercoverage.
This is not a standard bias term, and the concern is that non-English speakers are left out of the sample entirely.
Random assignment is an experimental design feature, not a bias, and no treatments are assigned in a survey.

items.prompt: Why is random assignment used in an experiment?
choices: It guarantees that every participant receives the preferred treatment.
It allows the researcher to generalize to every population.
It tends to balance lurking variables across treatment groups.
It prevents the response variable from varying.
items.rationale: Random assignment reduces systematic differences among treatment groups and supports cause-and-effect conclusions.
choiceRationales: Random assignment uses a chance mechanism so participants cannot choose their group, preventing preference from confounding results while roughly balancing uncontrolled variables.
Broadening conclusions to a larger population requires random sampling from that target population, whereas random assignment to treatments supports causal inference among study subjects.
Best answer. Random assignment reduces systematic differences among treatment groups and supports cause-and-effect conclusions.
The response still varies; random assignment makes group differences attributable to treatment rather than lurking variables.

items.prompt: A study compares two study schedules. Students are first grouped by prior GPA, then randomly assigned to schedules within each GPA group. The GPA groups are called what?
choices: Parameters
Clusters
Sampling frames
Blocks
items.rationale: Blocking groups similar experimental units before random assignment to reduce variation from a known source.
choiceRationales: A parameter is a numerical summary of a population; the GPA groups are sets of students, not numbers.
Clusters are groups selected whole in a sampling design; here the groups exist to control variation before random assignment.
A sampling frame is the list from which a sample is drawn; it is not a grouping used inside an experiment.
Best answer. Blocking groups similar experimental units before random assignment to reduce variation from a known source.

items.prompt: In a placebo-controlled experiment, neither participants nor the staff measuring outcomes know which treatment each participant received. What feature is present?
choices: Double-blinding
A census
Undercoverage
A matched-pairs sample without treatment
items.rationale: Keeping both participants and outcome assessors unaware can reduce placebo effects and measurement bias.
choiceRationales: Best answer. Keeping both participants and outcome assessors unaware can reduce placebo effects and measurement bias.
A census is collecting data from an entire population; blinding is about who knows the treatment assignment.
Undercoverage is a sampling problem where some people cannot be selected, not a feature of treatment concealment.
Matched pairs describe a design structure, and this experiment does impose treatments; the feature described is double-blinding.

items.prompt: A random sample of 500 app users reports their weekly screen time. Which conclusion is justified if the sample was representative?
choices: The sample proves that the app itself caused the reported screen time.
Results can generalize to the broader population of similar people.
The result automatically applies to every single person in the country.
The sample statistic is exactly equal to the population parameter itself.
items.rationale: Random sampling supports generalization to the sampled population, but an observational survey does not establish causation and statistics are estimates.
choiceRationales: A survey observes behavior without assigning treatments, so it cannot establish that the app caused anything.
Best answer. Random sampling supports generalization to the sampled population, but an observational survey does not establish causation and statistics are estimates.
The sample was drawn from app users, so generalization reaches similar app users, not the whole country.
Even a well-chosen random sample introduces sampling variability, so the sample mean estimates the true population parameter with a margin of error rather than matching it exactly.

items.prompt: Adding the same constant to every observation in a data set changes the mean but leaves which quantity unchanged?
choices: The median of the data
The minimum of the data
The standard deviation
The maximum of the data
items.rationale: Adding a constant shifts location summaries but does not change distances among observations, so standard deviation remains unchanged.
choiceRationales: Adding a constant shifts every value, including the middle one, so the median increases by that constant.
Adding a constant to every observation shifts all position summaries upward by that same constant, so the smallest value moves directly alongside the mean and median.
Best answer. Adding a constant shifts location summaries but does not change distances among observations, so standard deviation remains unchanged.

items.prompt: If p = 0.40 and n = 100, what is the standard deviation of the sample proportion, assuming the conditions are met?

items.prompt: A confidence interval for mu1 − mu2 is (−3.1, 1.4). What conclusion is supported?

The second population mean is definitely the smaller of the two means.
There is not convincing evidence that the population means differ.
The two sample means must be exactly equal to one another here.
items.rationale: Because zero is in the interval, a zero population difference remains plausible; the interval does not prove equality.
choiceRationales: Because the interval (−3.1, 1.4) extends above zero as well as below it, mu1 could plausibly be greater than or equal to mu2, so no definite ordering is supported.
Because the interval (−3.1, 1.4) includes negative values and zero, mu1 could plausibly be smaller than or equal to mu2, leaving no convincing evidence of a difference.
Best answer. Because zero is in the interval, a zero population difference remains plausible; the interval does not prove equality.
The interval is centered at −0.85, so the sample means differ; the question is about the populations.

items.prompt: Which design calls for a matched-pairs t-test rather than a two-sample t-test?

Two categorical variables from one population are compared.
A single proportion is compared with a target value.
The same 24 people are tested before and after treatment.

choiceRationales: Measuring unrelated individuals in two separate groups creates independent samples with no natural pairing, which calls for a two-sample t-test rather than a matched-pairs procedure.
Investigating an association between two categorical variables recorded on one sample requires a chi-square test of independence rather than any t-test for quantitative means.
Testing whether one population proportion differs from a specified benchmark uses a one-proportion z-test rather than a matched-pairs t-test for quantitative differences.

items.prompt: A two-sample t-test for mu1 − mu2 has p = 0.004. At alpha = 0.01, what is the correct conclusion?
choices: Fail to reject the null hypothesis because 0.004 is greater than the 0.001 cutoff here.
Reject the null; data show convincing evidence of a mean difference.
Accept the null hypothesis as having been proven true by this one particular sample.
Conclude that every individual in group 1 exceeds every individual in group 2 here.
items.rationale: The p-value is below alpha, so the result is statistically significant; the conclusion must stay about population means, not every individual.
choiceRationales: The specified significance level is alpha = 0.01 rather than 0.001; since the p-value of 0.004 is smaller than 0.01, the correct decision is to reject H_0.
Best answer. The p-value is below alpha, so the result is statistically significant; the conclusion must stay about population means, not every individual.
A p-value of 0.004 is strong evidence against H_0 at alpha = 0.01, and even with a large p-value a significance test never proves a null hypothesis true.
A two-sample t-test makes an inference about the difference between population averages, whereas individual observations from the two populations can still overlap substantially.

items.prompt: A least-squares line is y-hat = 12 + 4x. What is the predicted response when x = 5?

items.prompt: If two events are mutually exclusive and both have positive probability, can they be independent?
choices: Yes, because every mutually exclusive pair is independent.
Yes, if their probabilities sum to more than 1.
Only if both probabilities equal 0.50.
No; if one occurs, the other becomes impossible.
items.rationale: Positive-probability mutually exclusive events cannot be independent because the occurrence of one changes the conditional probability of the other to zero.
choiceRationales: Mutually exclusive events with positive probability are never independent, since one occurring rules the other out.
Mutually exclusive probabilities cannot sum to more than 1, and the sum has nothing to do with independence.
Two mutually exclusive events with probability 0.50 each still cannot be independent; P(A and B) would be 0, not 0.25.
Best answer. Positive-probability mutually exclusive events cannot be independent because the occurrence of one changes the conditional probability of the other to zero.

items.prompt: If P(A) = 0.30 and P(B | A) = 0.40, what is P(A and B)?
items.rationale: By the general multiplication rule, P(A and B) = P(A)*P(B | A), which holds whether or not events are independent. Multiplying 0.30 by 0.40 gives 0.12.
choiceRationales: Best answer. By the general multiplication rule, P(A and B) = P(A)*P(B | A), which holds whether or not events are independent. Multiplying 0.30 by 0.40 gives 0.12.
0.10 subtracts 0.30 from 0.40, but finding the joint probability P(A and B) requires the general multiplication rule P(A) * P(B | A) = 0.30 * 0.40 = 0.12 rather than subtraction.
0.70 adds P(A) and P(B | A), which conflates a conditional probability with a mutually exclusive union; a joint occurrence of A and B is computed by multiplying 0.30 by 0.40.
1.33 divides 0.40 by 0.30 and exceeds 1, which is impossible for any probability; the general multiplication rule multiplies P(A) by the conditional probability P(B | A) instead.

items.learningObjectiveLabel: Conditional Probability
items.learningSectionLabel: Probability and Random Variables: study route 2

items.prompt: If P(A) = 0.60 and P(B) = 0.50, what value of P(A and B) would be consistent with independence?
items.rationale: Two events are statistically independent if and only if P(A and B) = P(A)*P(B). With P(A) = 0.60 and P(B) = 0.50, independence requires P(A and B) = 0.60(0.50) = 0.30.
choiceRationales: 0.10 takes the difference 0.60 - 0.50, whereas two events are independent only when their joint probability equals the product P(A) * P(B), giving 0.60 * 0.50 = 0.30 here.
Best answer. Two events are statistically independent if and only if P(A and B) = P(A)*P(B). With P(A) = 0.60 and P(B) = 0.50, independence requires P(A and B) = 0.60(0.50) = 0.30.
0.55 averages P(A) = 0.60 and P(B) = 0.50 rather than multiplying them; under independence, P(A and B) must equal P(A) times P(B), which cannot exceed either individual probability.
1.10 sums 0.60 and 0.50 to a number greater than 1, which violates probability bounds; checking independence requires multiplying P(A) and P(B) to obtain an intersection probability of 0.30.

items.prompt: A random variable has E(X) = 8. Which statement about its standard deviation is correct?
choices: Its standard deviation must equal 8.
Its standard deviation must be negative.
Its standard deviation measures spread around 8.
Its standard deviation determines the most likely outcome.
items.rationale: Expected value gives the center of a probability distribution, while standard deviation measures its typical spread around that center.
choiceRationales: The center and the spread are separate quantities; knowing E(X) says nothing about the standard deviation.
Standard deviation is defined as the square root of the average squared deviation from the mean, so it is always zero or positive and describes typical distance from E(X) = 8.
Best answer. Expected value gives the center of a probability distribution, while standard deviation measures its typical spread around that center.

Standard deviation summarizes typical spread around the expected value of 8, not the mode; identifying the most probable outcome requires inspecting the individual probabilities in the distribution itself.

items.prompt: For X ~ Binomial(20, 0.30), which expression represents P(X = 0)?
items.rationale: Zero successes means all 20 trials are failures, each with probability 0.70, under the binomial conditions.
choiceRationales: 20(0.30) = 6 computes the binomial mean np, not a probability; getting zero successes in 20 independent trials requires multiplying the failure probability 1 - 0.30 = 0.70 across all 20 trials.

1 - (0.70)^20 is the complement of P(X = 0) and therefore gives the probability of at least one success, whereas zero successes requires all 20 trials to fail directly.

18 is the population standard deviation for individual observations, whereas averages of 81 values vary much less and have standard error sigma / sqrt(n) = 18 / 9 = 2.

items.prompt: A residual plot has a clear curved pattern. What does this suggest about a linear model?

items.prompt: If r-squared = 0.72, what percentage of response variation is not explained by the fitted linear model?

About 28%

items.prompt: A confidence interval for the slope contains 0. What is a cautious conclusion?

The population slope has been proven to be exactly zero in the entire population here.
The two variables are proven to be independent in every possible population studied here.
The fitted model proves that a real causal effect exists between the two variables here.
items.rationale: An interval containing zero leaves a zero slope plausible; it does not prove no association or establish causation.
choiceRationales: Best answer. An interval containing zero leaves a zero slope plausible; it does not prove no association or establish causation.
Zero is merely one plausible value inside the confidence interval alongside other nonzero slopes, so capturing 0 never proves the true population slope equals zero exactly.
Lack of evidence for a slope is not proof of no relationship, and the result applies only to the sampled population.
Because 0 lies inside the interval, the data do not even establish a nonzero linear relationship, and observational regression slope intervals can never by themselves prove causation.

items.prompt: A p-value of 0.48 is obtained. Which statement is accurate?

items.prompt: Which change can reduce the probability of a Type II error when other design choices remain appropriate?

Use a biased sampling method.
Remove the response variable.
Increase the sample size.

Eliminating the response variable leaves no outcome to measure or test statistically; reducing Type II error means improving power through larger sample size, higher alpha, or lower noise.

items.prompt: Which factor generally makes a two-proportion confidence interval narrower?

A higher confidence level with no other change.
More variability in the estimates.
Replacing random samples with volunteers.

items.prompt: A one-sample t-test has p = 0.08 at alpha = 0.05. Which conclusion is appropriate?

The alternative is proven false.
Not statistically significant at the 5% level.
The test has no sampling variability.
items.rationale: Because p exceeds alpha, the evidence is insufficient to reject the null at the stated level.
choiceRationales: With p = 0.08 exceeding alpha = 0.05, we simply fail to reject H0 for lack of convincing evidence; failing to reject never proves that the population mean matches the null value.
A p-value of 0.08 means the sample data are not rare enough at the 5% significance level to reject H0, which leaves the alternative unconfirmed rather than disproved.

items.prompt: If independent sample sizes are increased while population variability stays fixed, what generally happens to the standard error of a difference in means?

It becomes equal to the population means.
It becomes negative.
It decreases.
items.rationale: Larger independent samples reduce the variability of each sample mean and therefore of their difference.
choiceRationales: In sqrt(s1^2/n1 + s2^2/n2), both sample sizes sit in the denominators, so enlarging n1 and n2 while variability stays fixed makes the standard error shrink toward zero rather than grow.

The response variable is a single categorical label in each group.
Each person contributes a single before-and-after pair of values.
The two groups were selected by voluntary response alone here.

choiceRationales: Best answer. A two-sample t interval targets a difference in means for independent quantitative groups when conditions hold.

items.prompt: A boxplot has Q1 = 20 and Q3 = 32. At which value does the upper 1.5-IQR fence occur?
items.rationale: Tukey's upper outlier fence is Q3 + 1.5*IQR. First find IQR = Q3 - Q1 = 32 - 20 = 12, multiply by 1.5 to get 18, and add to Q3 = 32 to obtain 32 + 18 = 50.
choiceRationales: 38 adds only 0.5 * IQR (6) to Q3 = 32; since IQR = 32 - 20 = 12, the standard upper outlier fence uses Q3 + 1.5 * IQR = 32 + 18 = 50.
44 adds a single IQR (12) to Q3 = 32 instead of 1.5 IQRs; Tukey's upper fence rule multiplies the interquartile range 12 by 1.5 to add 18, giving 50.
64 doubles Q3 (32 + 32) instead of using the interquartile range 32 - 20 = 12; the upper fence is calculated as Q3 + 1.5(IQR) = 32 + 18 = 50.

limitations: This foundation pilot is not a complete AP Statistics exam simulation and does not reproduce the official digital exam experience.
Official free-response task forms, source sets, scoring rubrics, and score conversions are not included or scored.
No official score, readiness, college-credit, or psychometric inference is supported.

blueprint.officialSectionOne: 42 multiple-choice questions in 90 minutes; 50% of the official exam score.
blueprint.officialSectionTwo: 4 free-response questions in 90 minutes; 50% of the official exam score.

unitWeights.label: Unit 1: Exploring One-Variable Data and Collecting Data
Unit 2: Probability, Random Variables, and Probability Distributions
Unit 3: Inference for Categorical Data: Proportions
Unit 4: Inference for Quantitative Data: Means

blueprint.pilotAlignment: 240-item text-first foundation sampler across all five revised units and all fifty-five public framework topic IDs; forty-eight five-item internal banks; fifteen section-linked practice routes; four guided cumulative routes; transfer practice beyond the two-item topic floor; nine unscored constructed-response planning workshops; no official stimulus sets or FRQ scoring.

skills.label: Selecting Statistical Methods
skills.description: Select an investigative question and an appropriate statistical method for the data and goal.

skills.label: Analyzing Data
skills.description: Identify, represent, calculate, and compare statistical information needed to answer a question.

skills.label: Using Probability and Simulation
skills.description: Calculate or estimate probabilities, parameters, intervals, and inference results.

skills.label: Statistical Argumentation
skills.description: Describe distributions, interpret results, verify conditions, and justify a claim in context.
